tools.image-to-ascii.faqs.0.answer: ASCII art uses the density of different characters to mimic the brightness of an image — denser characters represent darker areas and sparser characters represent brighter ones.
tools.image-to-ascii.faqs.1.question: What does the width setting do?
tools.image-to-ascii.faqs.1.answer: The width (number of columns) determines how many characters the output uses. More columns mean more detail but a wider result; fewer columns produce a more abstract look.
tools.image-to-ascii.faqs.2.question: What does invert mean?
tools.image-to-ascii.faqs.2.answer: Invert flips the brightness mapping, using sparse characters for dark areas and dense characters for bright ones — useful for displaying on dark backgrounds.

tools.image-similarity.faqs.0.question: How is similarity calculated?
tools.image-similarity.faqs.0.answer: The RGB values are compared pixel by pixel. Two pixels are considered similar when their color difference is within the tolerance, and the similarity percentage is the proportion of similar pixels.
tools.image-similarity.faqs.1.question: What do MSE and PSNR mean?
tools.image-similarity.faqs.1.answer: MSE (mean squared error) is smaller when the two images are closer. PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) is measured in dB — above 30 dB generally indicates near-lossless quality.
tools.image-similarity.faqs.2.question: What happens if I increase the tolerance?
tools.image-similarity.faqs.2.answer: A larger tolerance treats pixels with small color differences as similar, so similarity increases. A smaller tolerance makes the comparison stricter.
tools.image-similarity.faqs.3.question: Can images of different sizes be compared?
tools.image-similarity.faqs.3.answer: Yes. The tool scales both images to the same size before comparing them pixel by pixel.
